Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Mountain Goat Management Area A (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Mountain Goats are found in the high alpine or subalpine ecosystems where escape terrain is abundant. The earliest 
surveys for mountain goats in Alberta in the 1970’s included only the eastern slopes. Since mountain goats can 
easily move across the continental divide and their habitat complexes overlap both British Columbia and Alberta, 
surveys have been completed on both sides of the jurisdictional boundary since 1980 in southern Alberta. Although 
mountain goats can be observed on Bighorn Sheep surveys in the winter, the preferred season for counting MOGO 
is during the summer months in order to classify juveniles (kids) from yearlings with the highest confidence.
The Mountain Goat Management Plan (Alberta Sustainable Resource Development 2003) expects that each Mountain 
Goat Management Area will be surveyed every year that animals are allocated. The southwest Alberta Mountain Goat 
Management Area A, including Wildlife Management Units (WMU) 400 and 402 and their adjoining British Columbia 
habitat, was last flown in 2018, except for portions of WMU 400 which had not been flown since 2011. A limited hunt 
was initiated in 2001, with three defined mountain goat hunting areas (GHA) in WMU 400 (GHA O, Q and R). In 2015, a 
hunting area in WMU 402 was opened (GHA U). In 2024, an additional hunting area in WMU 402 was opened (GHA T). 
The mountain goat hunt provincially is a once in a lifetime opportunity.
Survey Method
A focused Total Minimum Count survey method was used to survey known mountain goat complexes along the 
British Columbia/Alberta border (Figure 1). Complexes were identified from previous aerial mountain goat survey 
information, and extended over areas of higher likelihood of use along the continental divide. Mountain complexes 
were flown at several altitudes to ensure complete coverage of habitat, from treeline to peaks. While a Total Minimum 
Count does not provide confidence intervals, it allows trend comparison over years. To enable high sightability 
of MOGO, flights are planned during the cooler early morning hours and in winds less than 20km/hr. At each 
observation point, mountain goats were classified by sex and age was recorded to adult, kid, and yearling. Photos 
were captured during observation to aid in classification. Other ungulate, carnivore, and eagle species encounters 
were also documented.
Results
An AS350 B3 was used for the survey. The crew consisted of three observers and a pilot. Survey results are 
provided based on the Goat Survey Area (Table 1) and summarized based on the general location of the Goat 
Survey Area. Goat Survey Areas within the North of Highway 3 area include; 1-16 (Figure 1). Goat Survey Areas 
within the South of Highway 3 area include; 17-26 (Figure 1).

Conditions
Aerial flights were conducted beginning at 0615 hours and ended either when temperatures reached 20 °C at 
elevation or wind and rising heat conditions created excess turbulence. Wind speeds remained below 10 km/h 
throughout the flights, with only a brief thunderstorm interrupting the otherwise calm weather during the week. Due 
to the high pressure weather system and a long stretch of warm, still weather, the survey was completed in 5 survey 
days.
North of Highway 3
North of Highway 3 (survey areas 1-17 , Figure 1), a total of 124 mountain goats were observed within both the Alberta 
and British Columbia sides of the divide with seventy-five mountain goats observed on the Alberta side of the divide 
and 49 observed in British Columbia. Of the 75 mountain goats in Alberta, 69 were in hunting area T, while one 
mountain goat was in hunting area U. Due to the low number of mountain goats and/or kids observed, additional 
survey transects were flown in hunting area “U” and around Crowsnest Mountain.
In general, the population of mountain goats north of Highway 3 has declined by approximately 40 individuals. In 
addition, the distribution of mountain goats has changed since previous surveys, with an increase on Tecumseh 
Mountain, and a decrease on Crowsnest Mountain. The kids per 100 adult ratio averaged 25 for the northern half of 
the survey. While Crowsnest Mountain still had the highest number of mountain goats in one survey unit, it also had 
a very low ratio of kids to 100 adults, with only 5.
Other species observations that occurred in the survey units north of Highway 3 included 1 bald eagle, 6 golden 
eagle, 246 bighorn sheep, 27 elk, 24 mule deer, 1 black bear, and 1 grizzly bear.
South of Highway 3
South of Highway 3 (survey areas 18-26, Figure 1), a total of 225 mountain goats were observed within both the 
Alberta and British Columbia sides of the divide, with 113 mountain goats observed in Alberta and 112 in British 
Columbia. Of the 113 mountain goats in Alberta, 21 were observed within hunting area “O”, 56 within hunting area 
“Q”, and 12 observed within hunting area “R”.
In general, the survey units south of Highway 3 have remained stable, although the distribution of mountain goats 
has changed between survey years. An increase in the number of mountain goats observed in Waterton Lakes 
National Park on the north boundary since the 2018 survey, which was flown the year following the Kenow wildfire, 
may indicate population recovery in the area. Another interesting observation, was the mountain goats observed in 
the West Castle drainage during the Sage Creek fire in 2018 have returned to British Columbia during this survey. 
The kids per 100 adult ratio averaged 27 for the southern half of the survey.
Other species observations that occurred in the survey units south of Highway 3 included 2 bald eagle, 2 golden 
eagle, 379 bighorn sheep, 45 elk, 27 mule deer, one white tailed deer, and one wolverine.
